questions.question: What are clinicians' biggest pain points with documentation?

seeded.answer:
Documentation burden is a primary driver of burnout for physicians, ranking as the #1 self-selected contributor with 52% citing it, exceeding patient volume at 31% [1][2]. Specifically, 64% of physicians report completing documentation after hours, averaging 1.2 hours per day [1][2]. One physician stated, “I love this job. I do not love finishing my notes at 9pm after my kids are in bed. If AI fixes that, I'm in.” [3].

Registered Nurses expressed concern that AI-generated documentation might diminish their clinical narrative voice, with this being the top volunteered concern from 89 open-ended responses [4][5]. One ICU nurse said, “My notes are how I hand off a patient safely. If a robot writes them and I'm just rubber-stamping, that scares me more than typing.” [5].

questions.question: Why didn't physicians trust the ambient scribe's draft notes?

seeded.answer: Initially, physicians did not trust the ambient scribe’s draft notes because 4 of 5 participants read every line of generated text during the first exposure [1]. This behavior was observed in the v0.1 prototype in February 2025 and undercut the expected time-savings [1]. In early testing, medication dosages were missed or garbled in 3 of 5 sessions, leading physicians to state this was disqualifying without review [2]. Even after accuracy improved, reading behavior didn’t change, creating a “frustration plateau” where clinicians didn’t perceive a difference [3]. The personas indicate a key goal is to trust the tool without blindly accepting everything it generates [4]. While the system technically detected sound-alike medication names, the UI didn’t clearly communicate this, leading to reliance on a generic low-confidence signal [5].

sources.title: Usability Test — Ambient AI Scribe Prototype v0.1
sources.participants: Participants: 5 — Physician (Family Medicine), Physician (Internal Medicine), Nurse Practitioner
sources.excerpt:
[HIGH] (trust calibration) 4 of 5 participants read every line of AI-generated text before accepting it in this first exposure; none trusted it enough to skim, which undercuts the time-savings premise if that behavior persists post-adoption.
[MEDIUM] (interaction) Participants were unsure how to correct a single wrong sentence without regenerating the whole note; the edit affordance wasn't discoverable.
[MEDIUM] (workflow fit) The 'start listening' control required a manual click, which physicians said they would likely forget mid-conversation with a patient.

sources.participants: Participants: 5 — Physician (Family Medicine), Physician (Internal Medicine), Nurse Practitioner

[HIGH] (accuracy) The scribe correctly captured the chief complaint and HPI in all 5 sessions but missed or garbled medication dosages in 3 of 5 — physicians said this was disqualifying for direct sign-off without review.

questions.question: What did nurses want from the AI's citations?

seeded.answer: Nurses wanted inline citations to the specific chart text behind each AI suggestion, not just a black-box draft [1][2]. Specifically, they wanted to “see the chart text” supporting the AI’s claims [3][2]. In version 2 of the AI-assisted prior authorization drafting, citations linked to specific chart-text spans, allowing nurses to meaningfully check them [4]. This feature was directly added in response to a finding from the April 8th usability test with 4 utilization review nurses [3][2].

sources.title: AI-Assisted Prior Authorization
sources.excerpt:
AI-drafted prior authorization justifications were tested in two rounds (v1, Apr 2025; v2, Nov 2025) with the same utilization review nurse supervisor across both, which mattered for tracking whether fixes actually landed.
v1 surfaced a correctness bug (citing outdated diagnosis codes) serious enough that participants said it would likely cause payer denials — not a UX problem, a data-freshness/model fix. It also surfaced a durable requirement: nurses want inline citations to the specific chart text behind each suggestion ("show your work"), not just a black-box draft.

questions.question: What evidence supports making the calendar step required in onboarding?

seeded.answer: Evidence from 6 participants in usability sessions shows that step 3 ("Connect calendar") is frequently misinterpreted as optional [1][2]. Specifically, 2 of 3 participants in sessions 1-3 attempted to skip this step [1][3], and all participants in sessions 4-6 initially read it as optional [1][4]. One participant in session 1 explicitly questioned whether connecting a calendar was necessary, pausing for approximately 15 seconds before proceeding [5]. The Q1 Readout confirms step 3 is the largest drop-off point in the onboarding funnel [2]. Additionally, a heuristic evaluation identified a mismatch between the system and user expectations regarding the required nature of this step [6], and an accessibility screening found it to be a blocker for screen-reader users [7].

sources.title: Onboarding flow — setup step confusion
sources.excerpt: Sourced from raw/2026-01-19-onboarding-usability-test/ — 6 participants, moderated usability sessions, Jan 19–23 2026. In sessions 1–3, 2 of 3 participants tried to skip step 3 ("Connect calendar"): session 1 tried to exit via the step label, and session 2 tried to skip it before hitting the "required" indicator. Sessions 4–6 read the step as optional in the same way. The step 4 invite hesitation comes from session 3 ("I'm worried this is going to email my whole team before I'm ready") and the sessions 1–3 topline ( topline-summaries/example-topline-summary.md ).

This is independently corroborated by the Jan 2026 funnel export, which shows step 3 as the largest drop-off point in the wizard.

questions.question: What haven't we learned yet about care coordinators?

seeded.answer:
The sources indicate we haven’t learned about care coordinators’ needs regarding behavioral health or complex prior-auth cases [1][2][3]. Additionally, the research hasn’t fully addressed how to incorporate patient history into the alert ranking logic; the usability testing showed the current model prioritizes recency over coordinators’ understanding of patient history, leading to disagreements [4][5]. Five usability test participants disagreed with at least one ranking decision, and one stated they “wanted to tell it ‘no, this one’s more urgent because I know this patient’s history,’ but there was nowhere to put that” [6]. Three care coordinators reported manually cross-referencing 3-4 systems to understand a patient’s status [7].

questions.question: What is unresolved about the session timeout?

seeded.answer:
The current session lock state during active dictation is perceived as data loss by clinicians [1][2]. In a February 17, 2026 contextual inquiry, all four shadowed clinicians restarted dictation believing their draft was destroyed when the session locked, despite the draft being preserved server-side [1]. This misinterpretation stems from the UI not explicitly communicating that the draft is saved [1].

IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle timeout policy is fixed and cannot be adjusted [3][2], but also stated the UI messaging during the timeout is a product decision and can be changed [2]. The issue isn’t the timeout itself, but the lack of a clear “paused, draft preserved” state in the user interface [1][4]. The encounter view currently has a “locked (session timeout)” state [5], and SSO/MFA login has a “session-timeout-warning” state [6], but these don’t address the specific problem during active dictation.
